name: TLV9004IPWR
title: TLV9001, TLV9002, TLV9004: low-power 1-MHz op amps with rail-to-rail inputs and outputs
summary: Single, dual and quad CMOS operational amplifiers for 1.8 V to 5.5 V supplies, with inputs that reach 100 mV past both rails and outputs that swing to within tens of millivolts of them. Each channel draws about 60 µA and gives 1 MHz gain bandwidth, 2 V/µs slew rate, ±0.4 mV typical offset and 5 pA bias current. The S versions add active-low shutdown pins that cut the current below 1 µA and leave the outputs high-impedance. TLV9002IDDFR is the dual in the 8-pin SOT-23-THIN (DDF) package on tape and reel.
key_figures: ±0.4 mV typ, ±1.6 mV max at VS = 5 V

circuits.title: Single-pole low-pass filter
circuits.description: A noninverting amplifier with an RC low-pass in front of it. R1 and C1 set the corner, and RF over RG sets the passband gain of 1 + RF/RG.

circuits.title: Low-side current sensing
circuits.description: The load current returns to ground through a 0.1 Ω shunt. One amplifier of a TLV9002 on a 5 V supply amplifies the shunt voltage with a noninverting gain of 1 + 57.6 kΩ / 1.2 kΩ = 49 V/V, so 0 A to 1 A gives about 0 V to 4.9 V at VOUT.
notes: Design targets: load current 0 A to 1 A, output 4.9 V, shunt voltage at most 100 mV.

circuits.title: Single-supply photodiode amplifier
circuits.description: A transimpedance amplifier on 3.3 V. The photodiode, modelled as a 0 µA to 10 µA current source with 47 pF across it, drives the inverting input; RF = 309 kΩ turns the current into voltage and CF = 10 pF across it sets a 50 kHz bandwidth. R1 and R2 divide the supply to about 100 mV, which goes to the noninverting input so the output sits at VREF with no light and rises to 3.2 V at 10 µA. RL is a 10 kΩ load.
notes: Design targets: supply 3.3 V; photodiode current from 0 µA up to 10 µA; output swing 0.1 V up to 3.2 V; 50 kHz bandwidth.
IIN draws its current out of the INM node through pin 1 and returns it to ground at pin 2.

circuits.title: Input current protection
circuits.description: A unity-gain follower with a 5 kΩ resistor in series with the noninverting input. The resistor holds the current through the input clamp diodes to 10 mA or less when VIN goes past a supply rail.

circuits.title: Dual noninverting amplifier for the layout example
circuits.description: Both amplifiers of a TLV9002, each a noninverting stage with RG to ground and RF from output to inverting input. A low-ESR ceramic bypass capacitor sits at each supply pin, V+ to ground and V– to ground.

operation.text: TLV9001 is a single, TLV9002 a dual and TLV9004 a quad CMOS op amp for 1.8 V to 5.5 V supplies, with inputs and outputs that reach both rails, 1 MHz unity-gain bandwidth and about 60 µA per channel. The S versions (TLV9001S, TLV9002S, TLV9004S) add shutdown pins. All are specified from –40°C to 125°C; automotive versions are TLV9001-Q1, TLV9002-Q1 and TLV9004-Q1.
The TLV9001 comes in two five-pin orders: the DBV SOT-23 and the TLV9001T in SC70 put OUT on pin 1; the DCK SC70, the DRL SOT-553 and the TLV9001U in SOT-23 put IN+ on pin 1 and OUT on pin 4.

The amplifiers are stable at unity gain. They drive 500 pF of load capacitance, and because the open-loop output impedance is resistive, larger capacitive loads are easier to stabilize. The class-AB output can drive loads of 10 kΩ or less returned to any voltage between V+ and V–.
Each input has an integrated RFI and EMI filter, and the output does not reverse phase when the inputs are overdriven.

The part runs from 1.8 V to 5.5 V (±0.9 V to ±2.75 V). Several limits, among them offset, supply current, input offset current and output short-circuit current, apply across –40°C to 125°C; figures that move strongly with supply or temperature are given as typical curves. There is one operating mode: the amplifier is on whenever the supply is within that range.

The common-mode range runs 100 mV past each rail over the whole 1.8 V to 5.5 V supply range. Two input pairs work side by side: a P-channel pair covers inputs from 100 mV below V– up to about (V+) – 1.4 V, and an N-channel pair covers from about (V+) – 1.4 V to 100 mV above V+. Both pairs conduct in a transition band, typically (V+) – 1.2 V to (V+) – 1 V; with process spread the band can sit anywhere from (V+) – 1.4 V to (V+) – 1.2 V at its low end and from (V+) – 1 V to (V+) – 0.8 V at its high end. Inside that band PSRR, CMRR, offset, offset drift and THD can be worse.

The output stage is class AB built from common-source transistors, which lets it swing to the rails. With a 10 kΩ load the output comes within 20 mV of either rail at any supply voltage; other loads change how close it gets.

Internal filtering reduces the effect of RF interference from radios and from digital circuits on the same board. EMI rejection was measured from 10 MHz to 6 GHz; EMIRR IN+ is 59.5 dB at 400 MHz rising to 88.8 dB at 3.6 GHz.

Overload recovery is the time the output takes to come out of saturation back into linear operation after an input or gain drives it past the rails. Once out, the output slews at the normal slew rate, so the total delay after an overload is the recovery time plus the slewing time. The recovery time is about 850 ns.

TLV9001S, TLV9002S and TLV9004S have active-low SHDN pins that put the amplifier into standby, where it typically draws under 1 µA. The pins are referred to V–; the switching threshold is about 620 mV typical above V–, does not move with supply voltage, and has hysteresis. A valid low is V– to V– + 0.2 V and a valid high is V– + 1.2 V to V+. An internal pull-up to the positive supply enables the amplifier when the pin is left open; driving the pin to a valid level is preferred. The pin must not go above (V+) + 0.5 V, or the part is damaged.

The SHDN inputs are high-impedance CMOS. Each amplifier of a dual has its own pin (the DSBGA dual has one pin for both); a quad has one pin per pair. Enable takes 70 µs from full shutdown of all channels and disable takes 4 µs. A disabled output goes high-impedance, so TLV9002S and TLV9004S outputs can share an analog bus or act as gated amplifiers. The disable time depends on the load and grows as the load resistance rises; the specified tOFF needs the 10 kΩ load to mid-supply, and with no load turn-off is much slower.

Use 0.1 µF bypass capacitors close to the supply pins to cut coupling from noisy or high-impedance supplies. Supply voltages above 6 V can permanently damage the part; the absolute maximum rating is 7 V.

All pins have internal ESD protection; at the inputs and output it is mainly steering diodes to the supply pins. These diodes also protect against input overdrive as long as the current stays at or below 10 mA, which a series input resistor can ensure. That resistor adds thermal noise, so in low-noise circuits it should be as small as possible.

Put low-ESR 0.1 µF ceramic capacitors from each supply pin to ground as close to the part as possible; with a single supply one capacitor from V+ to ground is enough. Keep analog and digital grounds separate and watch where ground current flows; a ground plane on one or more layers spreads heat and reduces EMI pickup.

Route input traces away from supply and output traces; where they must cross a noisy trace, cross at 90 degrees rather than running in parallel. Keep inputs short and place RF and RG right at the inverting input to hold down parasitic capacitance. A driven low-impedance guard ring around sensitive traces cuts leakage from nearby nodes at other voltages. Clean the board after assembly; after any aqueous cleaning, bake the assembly to drive out moisture taken up by the plastic package, for example 30 minutes at 85°C.
The gain depends only on the RF to RG ratio. Their absolute size sets the impedance level, which decides the current they draw and how much stray capacitance matters; no one level suits every design.
